title: Transient-pool degradation safety and graceful invoice allocation for temporary boosts
creator: Marco Li
description: Problem statement: customer's Dedicated fleets can take temporary capacity boosts from surge pools (operator- or policy-triggered). When surge capacity is reclaimed or the pool is degraded (node preemption, AZ outage, or autoscaler reclaim), workloads see capacity delta that can cause throttling or order-of-magnitude latency increases. Current billing allocates the full boost cost to the customer for the entire boost window, leading to disputes when boosts were partially used or revoked for platform remediation. This ticket defines a safe degradation behavior for transient boost drains and an invoice allocation model to reduce customer surprise and operator friction.
acceptance_criteria: A1: When a customer's temporary boost is revoked mid-window, billing is pro-rated by actual served capacity minutes with clear line items in invoice APIs and Console

A2: During staged degradation of a surge pool (planned or emergent), there is a 3-phase soft-degrade: announce -> graceful-drain -> hard-reclaim; customers receive route-level throttling signals and per-route fallback attempts are logged
A3: Autoscaler/backoff policy updates prevent instant eviction of in-flight KV-cache sessions and maintain per-request SLOs where feasible (documented behavior in runtime-1.20 release notes)
A4: Console shows a timeline for boost lifecycle and a revisionable allocation reason (operator action, preemption, policy timeout)
A5: E2E load test (synthetic) reproduces degrade scenario and meets target: 95th pct latency increase <= 2x baseline for top-10 routes during soft-drain phase
technical_notes: Introduce a BoostLease object in control plane with start_ts, intended_end_ts, and current_state (active, soft_draining, reclaimed). BoostLease changes are emitting structured audit events for billing reconciliation.

Implement minute-granular metering in surge backplane: track served GPU-minutes attributable to boost-weighted requests. Use existing token attribution headers to map requests to boost vs committed capacity.

Autoscaler change: when pool-level signal 'soft_draining' is set, new allocation decisions should prefer short-lived queueing (prefetch window) and reduce batch sizes for affected worker groups to minimize tail increases.
Billing: create invoice line types 'boost-grant', 'boost-used-pro-rating', and 'boost-refund' (negative line) to capture partial use. Expose breakdown in /invoices and Console export CSV.

Operator controls: add an operator action 'revoke-boost' that transitions BoostLease -> soft_draining for configurable grace window (default 5 minutes) before hard_reclaim. Revocations must be reversible within the grace window.
Instrumentation: add new metrics: boost_lease_count, boost_served_gpu_minutes, boost_revoke_rate, boost_soft_drain_95_latency_ratio. Dashboards: Billing Reconciliation and Surge Health.
Backwards compatibility: default behavior remains unchanged for customers not using temporary boosts; API surface additions are additive and opt-in for admin operators.
rollout_plan: 1) Spike/PR (ENG-50901-spike): implement BoostLease proto + control-plane hooks and unit tests (feature-flagged)
2) Internal dogfood: enable in sandbox fleet and run synthetic degrade scenarios against 3 tenants for two weeks
3) Billing integration: connect minute-granular metrics to billing pipeline (accounting team review), run reconciliation pairwise on last 90 days backlog
4) Console: add Boost timeline UX behind feature flag; ship with dedicated-2026.04 canary
5) Gradual rollout: 10% of operator-initiated revokes routed to new graceful path for 48h, monitor errors and disputes
6) Full rollout and docs: publish operator runbook and customer-facing docs including example invoices and dispute flow
risks: Billing complexity introduces reconciliation bugs; need end-to-end tests and manual audits for initial runs
Telemetry gaps could misattribute requests (edge cases during multi-tenant GPUs), causing over/undercharging
Grace window too short -> SLO violations; too long -> wasted capacity and customer cost exposure
Operator UX complexity: making revoke reversible is required but increases race conditions; careful locking needed
